newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Up to 32 die in Russia blast, sabotage suspected.
newsitem.headline: Up to 32 die in Russia blast, sabotage suspected.

text.p: Up to 32 people were killed when an explosion destroyed a building housing Russian military officers in the southern republic of Dagestan on Saturday and officials have not ruled out sabotage, news agencies said.
Agencies and Russian radio stations put the death toll at between 23 and 32, but local and national branches of the ministry for emergency situations gave a lower figure.
"We can only confirm six people dead so far and seven more in hospital. Nineteen people have so far been dragged out of the rubble," a ministry spokeswoman in Moscow told Reuters.
About 58 people were in the eight-storey block when the explosion took place at 2.20 a.m. (2300 GMT), she added.
RIA news agency put the toll at 32 and said that at least five people had died after being taken to hospital, including a small child.
More than 130 people, mostly families of Russian border guards and air force officers, lived in the concrete-panel building in the port town of Kaspiysk by the Caspian Sea.
Cries for help could still be heard from the rubble in five or six spots by 2 p.m. Moscow time (1100 GMT), agencies said.
"Eleven cranes are removing rubble at the site and more rescue teams, including sniffer dogs, are on their way," another ministry spokesman Sergei Shoigu told Russian television.
The government vowed a swift investigation into the causes of the blast.

"I give my assurance that all necessary measures will be taken to uncover the reasons," Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said in a message of condolences to the families of the dead published by Itar-Tass news agency.
Dagestan borders the Caspian Sea and the breakaway Russian republic of Chechnya, where an uneasy peace is holding after a 21-month bloody conflict between Russian forces and Chechen separatists.

Some officials in Moscow said there could be a link between the blast and the Chechen peace process. Leonid Mayorov, deputy secretary of the powerful Security Council, called the explosion an attempt to derail peace talks, RIA news agency said.
The Interior Ministry said it had not ruled out the possibility of a terrorist action, Interfax reported.

Itar-Tass news agency, quoting General Vladimir Ruzlyayev of the regional border guards, said the blast was unlikely to be the result of a gas explosion because the house was not linked to the gas mains.
Tass quoted sources as saying there were signs that TNT had been exploded in the building and it said the presence of TNT was hampering rescue operations.
"Preliminary information indicates that an explosive device of unidentified type went off," it quoted a press officer of the Russian border guard forces as saying.

Viktor Ilyushin, a communist deputy in the State Duma lower house of parliament, blamed the explosion on Chechen rebels, although the authorities have so far not pinned the blame on any particular group.
"Chechnya cannot live in an enclosed space...It will carry its military offensive to Dagestan," Interfax quoted him as saying. Saturday's blast was clearly well-planned, he added.
"Today we are reaping the fruits of carelessness," he said.

Chechen rebels seized hundreds of hostages in the Dagestani town of Kizlyar early this year, in the second major raid outside the territory of the breakaway republic. Dozens of people were killed in the raid, but many of the rebels escaped.
Their 21-month armed conflict with Moscow has since ended with a peace deal signed on August 31.

On Saturday an aide to Chechen separatist leaders hammered out a temporary agreement with Russian officials aimed at mapping out relations between Moscow and its breakaway region in the period leading up to planned elections on January 27.
